title: The Lacquered Beasts of the Portage
summary: A craft settlement’s moving models explain a confederation’s broken logistics, while its real carriers contest the heroic story.
history: After a river dynasty collapsed in 758, rival commanders divided its landings among eighteen allied households. Their agreements failed to account for the portage connecting sheltered waters across a rain-soaked ridge. A sword assessor established a craft settlement there, bringing lacquer workers, gardeners, and puppet builders together. One builder made moving beast models whose incremental gestures demonstrated how loaded animals struggled on the track. Commanders commissioned grand performances of their victories while supplying too little food to real carriers. A southern advance stopped within sight of its destination because its crews and animals could carry no more. The craft records preserve practical limits obscured by the confederation’s succession chronicles.
question: whether portage households can set carrying limits against rulers who inherited toll rights but no credible maintenance duties.
transformations: Expertise spanning sword assessment, lacquer, pottery, and gardens becomes a craft settlement linked by patronage rather than one modern profession.
Sculpted models and incremental animation become hand-operated beast demonstrations and puppet sequences, using pre-industrial stage mechanics.
A fragmented post-dynastic settlement and rival claimants become eighteen landing households whose political arrangement neglects shared infrastructure.
An advance through difficult terrain outrunning its supplies becomes a portage campaign reconstructed through carriers’ accounts.
rows: Koresh of the Polished Edge

Koresh assessed blades but spent much of his stipend maintaining a communal garden. Patrons wanted verdicts of authenticity; workers needed usable tools. His workshop records distinguish prestigious old weapons from repaired blades fit for daily tasks.
The Rain Ridge Portage

Loaded boats cannot cross the ridge, so crews move cargo onto animals and sledges. Its mud changes with each storm. Military maps treat the passage as one line, concealing the unloading, feeding, and repair work that determines whether an expedition can proceed.
The Eighteen Landing Houses

The houses inherited separate toll rights after the dynasty fell. Their coordinated proclamations imply a common system, but no house accepts the expensive ridge repairs. Porters use that gap to negotiate a maintenance council independent of the rival commanders.
The Advance Within Sight

The southern force reached a ridge overlooking its destination with exhausted animals and empty grain sacks. Its retreat saved survivors but lost the campaign. Court chronicles blame weak morale; carriers’ accounts show a supply schedule impossible from the beginning.
The Jointed Burden Beast

A lacquered model bends incrementally under removable weights. Its maker used worn pack straps as hinges, making the demonstration mechanically honest. Patrons prefer a triumphant pose, while apprentices preserve the awkward movements that explain an animal’s limits.
The Blade and Root Inspection

Visitors inspect a repaired blade and a grafted tree before commissioning work. Both reveal care through later intervention. The custom challenges patrons who equate authenticity with untouched age, a preference that would condemn usable tools and living gardens alike.
The Porters’ Load Book

The book records load, weather, food, and rest instead of troop glory. It explains why equal weights produce unequal burdens. Commanders want fixed official limits; porters insist upon seasonal inspection rather than a convenient figure detached from the actual path.
The Mud Mane Grazer

These broad-backed grazers tolerate rain but need long feeding intervals. Commanders kept them saddled through nights to hurry departure, causing sores and collapse. Present keepers invoke the old campaign when refusing schedules that preserve appearances by damaging the animals.
The Seventeen Turns

The safest portage follows seventeen bends that officers repeatedly tried to straighten. Each bend avoids a steep drainage cut. Travelers who pay by distance favor shortcuts; carriers who pay with their bodies preserve the longer route and publish accident accounts.
The Burden Inspection Right

A carrier may demand inspection before accepting a load regardless of a commander’s sealed schedule. The right establishes a pause, not an unlimited refusal. Its survival depends on witnesses who can distinguish genuine danger from accusations of disloyalty.
Ovel the Small Beast Maker

Ovel learned anatomy by repairing hunting trophies and watching working animals. His stage patrons praised imagined monsters more than practical models. He used their fees to build demonstrations for porters, leaving an archive split between spectacle and useful observation.
The Lacquer Garden Compound

Workshops share a shaded garden that provides humidity control and food. Authorities classify the garden as ornamental to raise its assessment. Craftspeople document its practical uses, showing that beauty does not exclude a place from ordinary productive necessity.
The Ridge Strap Makers

Strap makers receive discarded hides and repair loops repeatedly rather than producing endless new harness. Toll houses seek exclusive supply contracts. Workers argue that seasonal scarcity requires flexible exchange with neighboring settlements, not perpetual promises to one patron.
The Division of Eighteen Cups

Commanders divided ceremonial water among eighteen cups while leaving the portage’s actual spring unassigned. The oversight caused decades of competing maintenance demands. A porter’s marginal note identifies the spring’s existing keeper, whom the grand ceremony never invited.
The Cup with No Landing

One confederation cup bears a landing name abandoned before the division. Its claimant collected tolls through the fiction of continuity. The cup’s authenticity is undisputed; the dispute concerns whether a genuine old object can authorize a right detached from any maintained place.
The Beast’s Failed Step

Puppet demonstrations end with a failed movement if the load exceeds the model’s balance. Sponsors want every performance to conclude successfully. The maker’s successors refuse, preserving failure as the part of the demonstration that makes safety negotiable.
The Eighteen Accounts Compared

The comparison reveals multiple houses charging for the same ridge repair. Some charges bought materials that never arrived. Its compiler distinguishes duplicated accounting from deliberate theft, permitting precise repayment claims instead of one satisfying accusation against the whole confederation.
The Lacquered Footprints

Wet prints appear beside stored beast models after storm nights. Workers find leaking roof channels in most cases, but one pattern persists under cover. They protect models from damp while recording the unexplained residue, avoiding damage in pursuit of either interpretation.
Garden Lacquer Preparation

Workers prepare resin in small shaded batches and discard contaminated material. Military buyers demand quantities beyond local fuel and labor. The craft council insists on bounded commissions, rejecting the assumption that prestige or ancestral favor can remove material limits.
The Toll Without the Ridge

Landing heirs claim tolls while denying responsibility for the track. Porters propose directing part of every collection to public maintenance. The negotiation threatens neither all inheritance nor all trade; it tests whether a continuing benefit can survive refusal of its practical cost.
